QUESTION

STATUS

EVIDENCE
R12 confirms all three remain on firmware 8. A retains its unchanged nine-hour pack; its only packet/latency results—99/100 and four seconds on firmware 7 (R03, Day 3)—became invalid after its Day 6 upgrade (R06), without demonstrating worse performance. Buffering remains disabled (R07). Its green READY badge reflects historical v1. B retains 119/120 packets, six-second latency (R04), enabled buffering (R07), and its 7.5-hour pack. The replacement order remains unfulfilled and unmeasured (R09–R12). C retains 198/200 packets, seven-second latency, enabled buffering, and eight-hour runtime (R10, Day 10).

QUESTION
Using the accepted current calibration, how many unique samples are late, out of how many unique samples? Name the late sample or samples.

EVIDENCE
# Canal telemetry replay

This is a synthetic telemetry investigation with a complete finite event catalogue. The cutoff is the end of Day 12. The incoming analyst must determine delivery performance, recover timings from the appropriate clock, and explain what a changed timing uncertainty would permit. All arithmetic uses seconds on a fictional reference timeline. The task concerns three unique acquired samples, S, T, and U. Transport retries do not create new acquired samples. Clock labels are part of the evidence; numbers copied from different clocks cannot be subtracted until their relation is applied. All intervals and acceptance thresholds in this history include their endpoints.

## C01 — Day 1, definition

A sample passes the delivery requirement if its true gateway arrival time minus its acquisition time is at most two seconds. Acquisition timestamps are already on the reference clock. Gateway timestamps use a different clock. The word delivery in this requirement means arrival at the gateway, not later insertion into a reporting database. Acquisition identifiers remain unchanged when a packet is retried. Every sample in the catalogue must be counted once. The analyst is asked to preserve enough detail to explain both a pass rate and a disputed individual sample.

## C02 — Day 2, dashboard draft

The first dashboard simply subtracts acquisition timestamps from the gateway's recorded timestamp. It labels differences above two seconds as late. The designer acknowledges that this is a provisional display awaiting clock calibration. It is useful for locating rows but is not yet an accepted lateness calculation. A separate graph shows database insertion times, which are intended for checking report backlog. Its title is shortened to receipt time in an early screenshot. The investigation retains that screenshot as historical context rather than silently treating the graph's title as a measurement definition.

## C03 — Day 3, sample S

Sample S is acquired at reference time 100 and has gateway recorded arrival timestamp 104. Its database insertion occurs at reference time 111. The row is intact, and no part of its payload is missing. The transport monitor marks it delivered because an arrival occurred; that mark does not itself decide whether the two-second latency requirement was met. The operator copies both timestamps into the investigation record. S is never retried, and there are no other observations with its acquisition identifier in the complete supplied catalogue.

## C04 — Day 4, sample T

Sample T is acquired at reference time 100.5 and has gateway recorded arrival timestamp 104.5. Its database insertion occurs at reference time 111, the same insertion time shown for S because the reporting process writes them together. The insertion batch therefore does not imply simultaneous acquisition or simultaneous arrival. The packet carries a different acquisition identifier from S and is a distinct sample. There is no retry for T. A chart that groups events by whole database insertion seconds is retained for backlog planning only.

## C05 — Day 5, sample U

Sample U is acquired at reference time 102 and has gateway recorded arrival timestamp 108. Its database insertion occurs at reference time 113. A retry envelope is later named U-retry, but it contains the same acquisition identifier and payload as U. It does not contain a new acquisition or a second first-arrival observation. The packet-level transport log counts this envelope as a second transmission. The sample-level service requirement counts only U once. The investigation must keep those denominators distinct when it translates the dashboard into a readiness report.

## C06 — Day 6, provisional count

An uncorrected screenshot shows four late rows: S, T, U, and U-retry. This is a faithful picture of what the provisional software displayed, not a verified statement that four unique samples violated the service requirement. One issue is clock calibration and another is retry identity. The analyst retains the screenshot to explain why the initial alarm was larger than the eventual sample catalogue. The number four should not disappear from the project history, but its meaning must not change from displayed rows to confirmed distinct failures.

## C07 — Day 7, clock calibration

The timing test establishes that the gateway clock was exactly three seconds ahead of the reference clock throughout all three arrivals. Thus a gateway reading g corresponds to reference time g minus three. The calibration covers the complete relevant arrival period; no drift or additional uncertainty applies in the current case. Acquisition timestamps need no correction. Database insertion timestamps also already use the reference clock. A technician's older guess of a one-second offset is withdrawn. This accepted calibration replaces that guess and governs the current performance calculation.

## C08 — Day 8, identity audit

The complete acquired-sample set is confirmed as S, T, and U. U-retry is an alias for U's retry envelope, not a fourth sample. No hidden samples are omitted, and no original acquisition has been excluded as invalid. Both envelope identifiers remain useful for tracing transport traffic. The service-level report, however, must use the three unique acquisition identifiers. The audit also confirms that the first gateway arrival values recorded in C03 through C05 are the ones to use, rather than the time a retry receipt was copied into the dashboard.

## C09 — Day 9, display repair

The developer plans two independent fixes: apply the accepted clock conversion and group transmissions by acquisition identifier. A preview changes the graph colors and rearranges the sample labels, but it does not add new measurements. The release ticket is still open, so screenshots from the deployed dashboard can continue to show the old provisional counts. The analyst can nevertheless calculate the required results from the preserved raw rows and calibration. A future display update is not a prerequisite for arithmetic, and a display preview is not an extra source of timing evidence.

## C10 — Day 10, contingency convention

The team records how to handle a future uncertainty interval for the offset. If the gateway is ahead by any amount o in a specified closed interval, an arrival reading g corresponds to the possible reference times g minus o. A guaranteed pass must meet the two-second requirement for every allowed offset. A guaranteed failure must exceed it for every allowed offset. An interval spanning a passing and a failing value supports neither guarantee. This convention does not replace the currently exact offset; it specifies how a changed assumption would be evaluated.

## C11 — Day 11, reporting scope

The incoming analyst should distinguish current observed lateness, the worst possible delay under a hypothetical uncertain offset, and the later database backlog. The report is not asked to estimate reliability for unseen samples or infer behavior on other days. S and T's shared insertion batch can be mentioned if explaining the display, but it is irrelevant to the current delivery threshold. The three seconds of calibration are a signed clock relation, not a processing delay that should be added to latency. The complete raw values remain available in the dated entries.

## C12 — Day 12, cutoff

There are no further samples, calibration changes, or amended raw timestamps. The current accepted offset remains exactly plus three seconds on the gateway clock. The complete sample set remains S, T, and U. The service threshold remains delay at most two seconds, including equality. The analyst will hand over both the factual current evaluation and enough of the conversion rule to assess a later explicit uncertainty change. Neither the unresolved display release nor the old screenshot changes the recorded sample identities or the accepted calibration.

QUESTION
If only the staff rental is adopted, does the A/B pair become feasible? Identify any remaining resource violations using the recorded quantities.

EVIDENCE
# Cedar shared-resource planning

This is a synthetic planning problem. All quantities are exact abstract units, not estimates for a real facility. The cutoff is the end of Day 12. The incoming planner must choose a feasible simultaneous pair, explain why earlier proposals changed, and reconsider the choice if a requirement or resource allowance changes. Three jobs are available: A, B, and C. Jobs are indivisible and run for the same full session. Their resource requirements add when run together. A job cannot borrow spare resources from a later session or split its work across time unless the question explicitly changes that rule.

## D01 — Day 1, goal

The initial goal is to run exactly two distinct jobs simultaneously and maximize their total output. There are three shared resource types: staff, memory, and power. A pair is feasible only if its summed requirements fit all three current caps at the same time. Feasibility is a supplied deterministic definition, not a probability estimate. Individual jobs can each be feasible while a proposed pair is not. The planner should retain enough of the alternatives to respond if a later request requires a particular job instead of simply maximizing the original objective.

## D02 — Day 2, job A

Job A needs four staff units, six memory units, and four power units for the session. It produces eight output units. Its setup is already complete and adds no further resource cost in this scenario. The team likes A because its output is easy to demonstrate, but preference does not change either its resource needs or the objective. These quantities remain fixed through the cutoff. A screen showing A alone reports it feasible under the provisional caps; that statement concerns the single job, not any pair containing it.

## D03 — Day 3, job B

Job B needs five staff units, five memory units, and five power units. It produces ten output units. The prototype schedule gives B the largest output label among the three jobs. It also lists a separate staff-only check to help the coordinator reserve people. That check is deliberately incomplete as a feasibility decision because memory and power are also shared. All three resource values apply simultaneously for the entire session. There is no option in the supplied catalogue to lower B's resource needs by accepting a smaller output.

## D04 — Day 4, job C

Job C needs three staff units, four memory units, and three power units and produces six output units. Its preparation note describes it as a possible companion for either A or B, depending on the caps. That wording is conditional rather than an approval of both pairs under every future budget. C is a distinct job and cannot be run twice to satisfy the two-job requirement. The project has no other job candidates. The incoming planner may therefore enumerate all three possible unordered pairs without assuming an unexplored external alternative exists.

## D05 — Day 5, provisional caps

The provisional shared caps are eight staff units, ten memory units, and eight power units. Each job fits by itself. An early slide highlights A and B because their separate outputs sum to eighteen, the largest unconstrained pair total. The slide was produced before the pair-resource calculation and is marked proposed. The pair's total requirements must be computed from both jobs. Neither an individual green badge nor the unconstrained output ranking establishes that this pair can run within the shared caps.

## D06 — Day 6, pair discussion

The team calculates candidate pairs and keeps the job-level requirements rather than only saving the winning name. A proposed rental would raise the staff cap, but it would not change memory or power. The rental quote is for staff capacity only. The coordinator explicitly rejects reading the phrase more capacity as an increase to every resource. The quote remains a proposal. No rental has been accepted, and the current staff cap is still eight. The project does not permit staff to substitute for missing memory or power units.

## D07 — Day 7, resource correction

The facility corrects the memory allowance from ten to nine units for the planned session. This is an adopted change and supersedes the earlier memory cap. The staff cap stays eight and the power cap stays eight. The correction changes the feasibility of some combinations without changing their output or job-level requirements. Old pair calculations under the ten-unit allowance are preserved with their date. They are useful for a future changed-budget question but cannot be silently reused as current approvals.

## D08 — Day 8, staff-only rental

The rental proposal is made concrete: it would raise the staff cap from eight to ten units, leaving the memory cap at nine and the power cap at eight. Its availability is assumed if a later question explicitly adopts it, but it is not adopted in the actual history. The rental has no output of its own and does not add a fourth job. A planner examining this option must recheck every limiting resource. Satisfying a previously tight staff inequality does not erase independent memory or power requirements.

## D09 — Day 9, alternative requirement

A stakeholder says that a future demonstration might require job A to be included. This request is not adopted for the current session; the present objective is still maximum output from any feasible pair. The coordinator asks the handoff to retain what would need to change if A later became mandatory. The project has no universal rule that the currently best pair remains best under a new inclusion requirement. The alternative must be evaluated from the original job requirements and whatever caps the new question actually supplies.

## D10 — Day 10, separate memory option

A separate option could add one memory unit, taking the adopted nine-unit cap back to ten. This option would leave staff and power at eight unless another change were separately specified. The option is not adopted before the cutoff. It must not be merged with the staff rental merely because both appear in the planning discussion. The two options affect different constraints and can be considered independently. The current plan includes neither option, and no resource measurement or job requirement is revised on this date.

## D11 — Day 11, reporting request

The incoming planner should state the selected pair, its total output, and its combined use of each resource. If asked about a rejected alternative, the explanation should identify the actual binding violations, not merely say it lost to another pair. If the objective changes, the planner should distinguish the original optimum from feasibility under the changed requirement. The finite catalogue is small enough that no search budget issue arises. A calculation that covers all three pairs is complete for this scenario, without claiming anything about larger scheduling problems.

## D12 — Day 12, cutoff

The final adopted caps are eight staff units, nine memory units, and eight power units. Job A still has requirements (4,6,4) and output 8; B has (5,5,5) and output 10; C has (3,4,3) and output 6, in staff, memory, power order. Exactly two distinct jobs must run simultaneously. No rental or extra memory has been adopted. The future A-inclusion request remains hypothetical. This final inventory is a convenient restatement of the primitives, not a replacement for the chronology explaining which earlier proposals and budgets are no longer current.

# Orchid listening workshop

This is a synthetic workshop-planning history with no real people or private records. The cutoff is the end of Day 12. The incoming coordinator must assess the current plan, explain remaining capacity, and decide whether a small attendance change fits the recorded rules. This is deliberately a straightforward case with a clear final restatement. A careful concise handoff should not invent hidden complications just because the chronology is long. The rules below are the whole feasibility rule for this exercise. Real-world requirements not stated here are outside scope and must not be added as reasons to approve or reject the plan.

## O01 — Day 1, activity

The workshop is a ninety-minute listening session using headphones and individual audio kits. The plan requires one kit per participant throughout the session. There is no kit sharing, and kits are not consumed during use. Leaders do not require participant kits. The program's purpose is to compare sound recordings, but the particular recording titles have no effect on the feasibility rule. The coordinator begins a chronological log so that room, staffing, and attendance decisions can later be summarized without requiring the successor to reread every design discussion.

## O02 — Day 2, room rule

The only available room has a participant capacity of twenty-four. Leaders do not count toward that participant cap in this fictional rule. The room is available from 09:00 through 17:00, with both endpoints allowed. An approved session must fit entirely inside that availability. There is no additional setup or cleanup time requirement in the exercise. A room booking and a staffing confirmation are separate records, though both are required. No other room is available, and there is no option to split participants across concurrent rooms.

## O03 — Day 3, leader rule

The workshop requires at least one confirmed leader for every twelve participants, so two confirmed leaders can support up to twenty-four participants. This is a supplied exact rule, not a real supervision recommendation. Fractional leaders are not possible. Two leaders are confirmed for the whole proposed session, and neither confirmation is later withdrawn. A third person offers to help with poster design but is not added as a leader. That offer does not increase staffing capacity and is unnecessary for the current attendance plan.

## O04 — Day 4, kit inventory

Twenty-four functioning audio kits are inspected and reserved for the workshop. The inventory includes exactly twenty-four usable participant kits; two empty shipping cartons are recorded separately and are not kits. The reservation remains valid through the cutoff. There is no later damage report or reassignment. The kit count is an independent capacity constraint even though its numerical value matches the room's participant cap. The incoming coordinator should be able to calculate spare kits from the current attendance rather than mistake the inventory count for the number of registered participants.

## O05 — Day 5, initial timing idea

An early poster draft proposes a 09:30 start. The program team later prefers 10:00 because that aligns better with arrival arrangements. The draft is retained in the design folder, but it is not a confirmed room booking. The room's general availability would permit either time for a ninety-minute session. A change of preferred start does not change the duration. The handoff should carry the final booked time and can omit the discarded poster layout unless explaining why an old flyer differs from the adopted plan.

## O06 — Day 6, confirmed booking

The room is confirmed for 10:00 through 11:30. This is the adopted session time and remains unchanged through the cutoff. Both leaders confirm that same full interval. The room's availability and the leaders' availability therefore cover the entire ninety-minute session. There is no break that would shorten either confirmation. The coordinator records the booking separately from the poster drafts. A future attendance change, by itself, does not move this booking or extend the session duration under the supplied rules.

## O07 — Day 7, audio arrangement

The venue prohibits amplified room sound before 11:00, but headphone listening is explicitly exempt. The workshop will use headphones throughout, with no amplified room playback. That plan remains unchanged through the cutoff. The recording selector briefly considers a speaker demonstration and then withdraws it before booking the equipment. The withdrawn idea is not part of the current activity. The headphone exemption matters if someone notices the early start and mistakenly applies the amplified-sound restriction to every kind of listening session.

## O08 — Day 8, attendance

Twenty-two participants are registered. This is the final actual attendance count in the history; there are no later cancellations or additions before the cutoff. Participants are the people counted against room capacity, kits, and the leader ratio. The two leaders are separate and do not use participant kits. A mailing list contains additional people who expressed interest but did not register. Its size is not an attendance forecast in this exercise and should not be added to the twenty-two registered participants when checking current feasibility.

## O09 — Day 9, design work

The team changes the poster from green to blue, shortens the workshop title, and switches the order of two recordings. None of these edits changes attendance, session length, kit needs, room capacity, staffing, or headphone use. The new poster is easier to read, but visual polish does not create a new approval requirement. The history retains the design decisions to resemble an ordinary project log in which operationally important events appear among ordinary work. A concise operational handoff can omit these edits without losing an answer to the stated task family.

## O10 — Day 10, contingency discussion

The coordinator expects possible requests for a small attendance increase and asks the successor to check every capacity rather than simply remember that the current plan passes. The room, kit inventory, and leader confirmations are fixed unless a future question explicitly changes them. Any added participants would use the same ninety-minute headphone session. There is no waiting-list priority rule to evaluate. A feasibility answer should say whether the requested total fits the supplied capacities; it need not decide whom to invite or send any invitations.

## O11 — Day 11, final operational synopsis

The adopted plan is twenty-two participants, twenty-four reserved functioning kits, two confirmed leaders with a twelve-participant capacity each, room participant capacity twenty-four, and a confirmed 10:00–11:30 session inside 09:00–17:00 availability. Headphones are used throughout and are exempt from the pre-11:00 amplified-sound restriction. Every required reservation and confirmation is complete. This synopsis intentionally brings the decisive facts together. It introduces no new rule and does not conflict with the earlier dated entries. The discarded timing and speaker ideas remain historical proposals only.

## O12 — Day 12, cutoff

No operational fact changes after the final synopsis. The current count remains twenty-two participants and the confirmed plan remains fully as stated in O11. The successor may use that synopsis to answer the current feasibility and spare-capacity questions without recovering the decorative history. A later explicit attendance increase should be checked against the same capacities. The exercise contains no unavailable source or unreported approval gate. Preserving the simple sufficient account is desirable; retaining every earlier design event would not automatically produce a better handoff.
